Why 100% RDA

A daily multivitamin is meant to fill the gaps a normal diet leaves, not to replace food or treat a deficiency. Dosing at the RDA covers the daily need while keeping every vitamin far below its upper limit, even when you also eat fortified foods such as atta, salt, oil or milk. Megadose multivitamins add cost and, for vitamins A and B6 in particular, the risk of excess over time.

Why these forms

  • Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) raises blood vitamin D more effectively than D2. See vitamin D3 + K2.
  • Vitamin K2 as MK-7 stays in the blood longer than K1 and pairs with D3 for bone health.
  • Methylcobalamin, L-methylfolate (5-MTHF) and P5P are active forms of B12, folate and B6 that do not need conversion. See vitamin B12.
  • Riboflavin-5′-phosphate is the active form of B2, and nicotinamide is a form of B3 that does not cause the flushing of nicotinic acid.
  • Retinyl palmitate provides preformed vitamin A at 90% of the RDA, leaving room for vitamin A from food.

What the vitamins do together

Together these vitamins contribute to normal energy-yielding metabolism, normal immune function, normal bones and teeth, normal skin and vision, normal nerve function, the formation of red blood cells, the protection of cells from oxidative stress and the reduction of tiredness and fatigue.

Best time to take a multivitamin

After a meal that contains some fat, because vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble. Breakfast is the easiest meal to make a habit, which is why the multivitamins are in the Day Pack, alongside the trace minerals and L-theanine + Panax ginseng.

Who should be careful

  • Warfarin or other vitamin K antagonists: vitamin K2 can reduce their effect. Do not use without your doctor's approval.
  • Pregnancy: use a prenatal supplement chosen with your doctor instead.
  • Other multivitamins or B-complex tablets: do not combine them with the Day Pack.
  • Methotrexate, some anti-seizure medicines and levodopa can interact with folate or B6. Ask your doctor.

What trace minerals do

  • Zinc contributes to normal immune function, skin, hair and nails, and fertility. See zinc picolinate.
  • Selenium contributes to normal thyroid function and the protection of cells from oxidative stress.
  • Iodine contributes to the normal production of thyroid hormones and normal cognitive function.
  • Copper contributes to normal connective tissue, iron transport and immune function, and balances zinc intake.
  • Manganese contributes to normal bone formation and energy metabolism.
  • Molybdenum contributes to the normal metabolism of sulphur amino acids.
  • Chromium contributes to normal macronutrient metabolism and the maintenance of normal blood glucose levels.

Why chelated forms

Minerals bound to amino acids or organic acids, such as zinc picolinate, L-selenomethionine and amino acid chelates, are generally well absorbed and gentle on the stomach compared with cheap oxides. Copper is included at 1.7 mg because long-term zinc intake can lower copper levels, and taking the two together keeps them in balance.

Why there is no iron

Iron competes with zinc for absorption, and most men and post-menopausal women do not need extra iron. Women with low iron or anaemia need a dose chosen by their doctor, so we leave iron out rather than guess.

Best time to take trace minerals

After breakfast, as part of the Day Pack. Taking minerals with food reduces the chance of nausea. Magnesium is taken separately in the Night Pack.

Who should be careful

  • Thyroid conditions or thyroid medicine: iodine and selenium affect thyroid hormones. Ask your doctor first.
  • Diabetes medicine: chromium may add to the effect of glucose-lowering medicines. Monitor your blood sugar and tell your doctor.
  • Antibiotics (quinolones, tetracyclines): take them 2 hours before, or 4–6 hours after, mineral supplements.
  • Wilson's disease or other copper disorders: do not take without medical advice.

The Super Routine Day Pack contains 200 mg of L-theanine and 200 mg of Panax ginseng root extract standardised to 3% ginsenosides. L-theanine is an amino acid from tea leaves studied for calm focus; Panax ginseng is studied for mental performance and fatigue. Neither contains caffeine. L-theanine: what the research says

L-theanine is an amino acid found naturally in tea. In a 4-week randomised trial in healthy adults, 200 mg a day improved stress-related symptoms and some measures of attention and sleep compared with placebo. Other small studies used 100–400 mg. The evidence is promising but limited, so we describe L-theanine as studied for calm focus, not as a treatment.

Panax ginseng: what the research says

Panax ginseng (Asian or Korean ginseng) is one of the most studied herbal ingredients. Trials have looked at mental performance, fatigue and wellbeing, mostly with 200–400 mg a day of standardised extract, with mixed but encouraging results. The NCCIH notes that the evidence is not conclusive. Standardising the extract to its ginsenoside content means each dose is consistent.

Why they are paired in the morning

Both fit the start of the day, when focus and energy matter, and neither is a stimulant. They sit in the Day Pack with the 13 multivitamins and 7 trace minerals.

Who should be careful

  • Pregnancy and breastfeeding: avoid Panax ginseng.
  • Diabetes medicine: ginseng may lower blood sugar. Monitor your levels and tell your doctor.
  • Warfarin and other blood thinners: ginseng may change their effect. Ask your doctor.
  • Antidepressants (MAOIs), stimulants or blood pressure medicines: ask your doctor before use.
  • Ginseng can cause sleep problems in some people, which is one reason it is taken in the morning.

FAQ

Does L-theanine make you sleepy?

Not at 200 mg in most people. It is studied for calm focus and relaxation without drowsiness, which is why it is in the morning sachet.

Does Panax ginseng contain caffeine?

No. Ginseng is a root and contains no caffeine.

How much L-theanine and ginseng is in Super Routine?

200 mg of L-theanine and 200 mg of Panax ginseng root extract standardised to 3% ginsenosides, in the Day Pack.

/ingredients/magnesium-glycinate/.h1: Magnesium glycinate: benefits, dose and when to take it
/ingredients/magnesium-glycinate/.inner:
Magnesium glycinate is magnesium bound to the amino acid glycine. It is gentle on the stomach and well absorbed. Most people take it in the evening. A 2000 mg dose gives about 280 mg of elemental magnesium, below the 350 mg daily upper limit for supplements. That is the amount in the Super Routine Night Pack.

Elemental magnesium: read this before comparing labels

Labels can be confusing. "1000 mg magnesium glycinate" is the weight of the whole compound, magnesium plus glycine. Only about 14% of that weight is magnesium itself. The figure that matters is elemental magnesium: 1000 mg of glycinate gives roughly 140 mg, and the 2000 mg in Super Routine gives roughly 280 mg. See elemental magnesium explained for every common form.

The adult Recommended Dietary Allowance is 400–420 mg a day for men and 310–320 mg for women, from food and supplements combined. The upper limit for magnesium from supplements is 350 mg a day. 280 mg covers about two-thirds of the adult requirement, tops up a diet that falls short, and stays below that limit.

What magnesium does

Magnesium is a co-factor in more than 300 enzyme systems. It contributes to normal muscle function, normal nervous system function, energy-yielding metabolism and the reduction of tiredness and fatigue. It also helps regulate calcium movement in nerve and muscle cells.

When to take magnesium glycinate

You can take it at any time, but most people take it in the evening with dinner or before bed. It fits a wind-down routine, and evening is when the Super Routine Night Pack is taken. Evidence that magnesium improves sleep is limited and mixed, and is strongest in people whose intake is low. We do not claim it is a sleep aid.

Many people pair it with melatonin; see melatonin and magnesium together for the evidence and safety rules.

We keep magnesium in the Night Pack and zinc in the Day Pack. Very high zinc intakes (around 142 mg a day) have been shown to reduce magnesium absorption. Our doses are far lower, but splitting the two removes any competition. See taking zinc and magnesium together.

  • Antibiotics (tetracyclines such as doxycycline; quinolones such as ciprofloxacin): take the antibiotic at least 2 hours before, or 4–6 hours after, magnesium.
  • Bisphosphonates for bone health (such as alendronate): separate by at least 2 hours.
  • Diuretics and long-term proton pump inhibitors (such as omeprazole) can change magnesium levels. Ask your doctor.

About 140 mg. Glycinate is roughly 14% magnesium by weight, so the 2000 mg in the Super Routine Night Pack gives about 280 mg.

Yes, for most healthy adults, if total magnesium from supplements stays below 350 mg a day. People with kidney disease should ask their doctor first.

Yes. Bisglycinate means one magnesium bound to two glycine molecules, which is what most labels mean by glycinate.

/ingredients/ashwagandha-ksm-66/.h1: Ashwagandha KSM-66: dose, timing and safety
/ingredients/ashwagandha-ksm-66/.inner:
KSM-66 is a full-spectrum ashwagandha extract made from the root only. Human trials have used 250–600 mg a day for stress and sleep, mostly for 8–12 weeks. The Super Routine Night Pack contains 600 mg of root-only extract, taken in the evening. Avoid it if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, or have thyroid or liver problems, unless your doctor agrees.

Studied range250–600 mg/day
Typical trial length8–12 weeks

What KSM-66 is

Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) is an Ayurvedic herb. KSM-66 is a branded extract made from the root only and standardised to its withanolide content. Generic ashwagandha powders vary, and some include leaf. A standardised extract means each dose is consistent.

What the research says

Several randomised trials found that ashwagandha root extract lowered perceived stress and cortisol compared with placebo. A 2021 meta-analysis found a small but significant improvement in sleep, larger in people with insomnia. The NIH Office of Dietary Supplements notes the limits: trials are small and short, most were run in India, and the extracts differ. We describe ashwagandha as studied for stress and sleep, not as a treatment.

300 mg vs 600 mg

KSM-66 trials on stress and sleep used 250–600 mg a day, and several of the trials with the clearest results used 600 mg, often split as 300 mg twice a day. We use 600 mg, the top of the range an international psychiatry taskforce suggested for anxiety (300–600 mg of root extract), and pair it with magnesium glycinate in the evening.

When to take ashwagandha

Trials gave it once or twice a day, morning or evening, so timing is flexible. We put it in the evening because the sleep studies are a key reason it is in the formula, and it fits a wind-down routine.

Who should avoid it

  • Pregnancy and breastfeeding: avoid. Several authorities advise against use.
  • Thyroid conditions or thyroid medicine: ashwagandha can change thyroid hormone levels. Speak to your doctor.
  • Liver disease: rare cases of liver injury have been reported. Stop and see a doctor if you notice yellowing skin, dark urine or abdominal pain.
  • Medicines for diabetes, blood pressure, immune suppression or sedation: ashwagandha may interact with them. Ask your doctor.
  • Hormone-sensitive prostate cancer: avoid unless your specialist agrees.

Safety beyond about 3 months has not been well studied. If you plan to use it for longer, review it with your doctor.

Is it better to take ashwagandha in the morning or at night?

Trials used both. Night suits a wind-down routine and the sleep studies, so it is in the Super Routine Night Pack.

KSM-66 is a root-only extract standardised to withanolides, so each dose is consistent. Generic powders vary in strength and may include leaf.

How long does ashwagandha take to work?

Most trials measured results after 8–12 weeks of daily use.

/ingredients/omega-3-rtg/.h1: Omega-3 (rTG): form, dose and the best time to take it
/ingredients/omega-3-rtg/.inner:
Omega-3 can be taken at any time of day. What matters is taking it consistently, and with a meal. The rTG (re-esterified triglyceride) form is absorbed somewhat better than the cheaper ethyl ester (EE) form. What EPA and DHA do

EPA and DHA are long-chain omega-3 fats from oily fish and algae. They are built into cell membranes, especially in the brain and eyes. EPA and DHA contribute to normal heart function, and DHA contributes to normal brain function and vision. Many Indian diets, especially vegetarian ones, contain little EPA or DHA.

Why 1000 mg of EPA + DHA

Health bodies suggest about 250–500 mg of EPA + DHA a day for general health. 1000 mg is in the range used in many studies on heart health and blood triglycerides, and well below the 5 g a day that US and European regulators consider safe from supplements. The figure that matters on a label is EPA + DHA, not total fish oil: a 1000 mg fish oil capsule often contains only 300 mg of EPA + DHA.

All three forms raise blood EPA and DHA. rTG gives a concentrated oil in a form closer to natural fish oil.

Best time to take omega-3: morning or night?

No study shows that one time of day is clearly better. Two things do matter:

  • Take it with a meal. Omega-3 is a fat and is handled like dietary fat, and taking it with food reduces fishy aftertaste and burps for many people.
  • Be consistent. Blood levels build over weeks of daily use, not hours.

We put omega-3 in the Night Pack so it is taken with dinner, usually the largest meal of the day in India. It also keeps the morning sachet small.

Either is fine. Take it with a meal and at the same time each day. We use dinner because it is usually the largest meal of the day.

rTG is absorbed somewhat better than ethyl ester (EE) concentrates, and is similar to natural fish oil. All forms raise EPA and DHA levels.

Plant foods such as flax provide ALA, which the body converts to EPA and DHA only in small amounts. Algae oil is a vegetarian source of DHA and EPA. The Super Routine Night Pack uses deep sea fish oil.

/ingredients/melatonin/.description: Melatonin explained: how it works, when to take 3 mg, what the evidence shows for sleep onset and jet lag, and who should not take it.
/ingredients/melatonin/.h1: Melatonin 3 mg: when to take it and how it works
/ingredients/melatonin/.inner:
Melatonin is the hormone that tells the body clock it is night. Take it 30–60 minutes before your usual bedtime. In studies it shortened the time to fall asleep in people with delayed sleep timing, and eased jet lag. 3 mg is a common adult dose. It is not for children or for anyone pregnant or breastfeeding.

Common adult dose0.5–3 mg
In Super RoutineNot included
When30–60 min before bed
Not forChildren, pregnancy

Not in the current formula. Earlier versions of Super Routine included 3 mg of melatonin in the Night Pack. The current formula does not. This guide stays online as general information. See what is in Super Routine now.

How melatonin works

The brain releases melatonin when it gets dark. It acts on MT1 and MT2 receptors in the body's master clock, which lowers alertness and shifts the body towards sleep. Bright screens late at night, irregular schedules and travel across time zones can all delay this signal.

What the research shows

  • Falling asleep: in people with delayed sleep timing, melatonin helped them fall asleep about 20–35 minutes sooner in reviewed studies, especially when combined with a fixed bedtime.
  • Jet lag: studies suggest it reduces jet lag symptoms after flights both east and west.
  • Chronic insomnia: evidence is weaker. Behavioural therapy (CBT-I) is the first-line approach.

When and how to take it

Take melatonin 30–60 minutes before your target bedtime, at about the same time every night, and dim screens and lights after taking it. Do not take melatonin in the morning or during the day.

Why 3 mg

3 mg is a widely used adult dose. Higher doses do not reliably work better and are more likely to cause next-day grogginess. Some people do well on less. If you feel drowsy the next morning, take it earlier in the evening and speak to a pharmacist.

Who should not take it

  • Children and teenagers, unless a doctor advises it.
  • Pregnant or breastfeeding women.
  • People with epilepsy, or taking blood thinners, sedatives or immunosuppressants: ask your doctor first.
  • People with dementia: guidelines advise against it.
  • Do not drive or operate machinery after taking melatonin.

Common side effects are mild: headache, dizziness, nausea and sleepiness. Long-term safety data are limited.

The Super Routine Night Pack does not contain melatonin. It contains magnesium glycinate, ashwagandha KSM-66 and omega-3 fish oil.

FAQ

How long before bed should I take melatonin?

30–60 minutes before your usual bedtime, at the same time each night.

Can I take melatonin and magnesium together?

Yes. They work in different ways and are commonly taken together in the evening. Check with your doctor if you take sedatives.

Is 3 mg of melatonin too much?

3 mg is a common adult dose. Higher doses are not reliably better and can cause morning grogginess. Some people need less.

Is melatonin habit-forming?

Melatonin is not considered habit-forming, but long-term safety has not been well studied. Use it as part of a consistent sleep routine.

/ingredients/vitamin-d3-k2/.h1: Vitamin D3 + K2: benefits, dose, best time to take it and why they pair
/ingredients/vitamin-d3-k2/.inner:
Take vitamin D3 with a meal that contains some fat, ideally at the same time each day. Breakfast works well for most people. D3 is fat-soluble and absorbs best with food. The Super Routine Day Pack contains 600 IU (15 mcg) of D3, which matches the adult daily recommendation, paired with 55 mcg of vitamin K2 as MK-7. Both are part of the Day sachet's 13 multivitamins.

Vitamin D3 + K2 benefits: why they matter in India

The skin makes vitamin D from sunlight, but indoor work, pollution, clothing, sunscreen and darker skin all reduce it. Low vitamin D status is common in India despite the sunshine. Vitamin D contributes to the normal absorption of calcium, normal bones and teeth, normal muscle function and normal immune function.

Why D3 and not D2

Both forms raise blood vitamin D, but D3 (cholecalciferol) raises and maintains levels more effectively than D2 (ergocalciferol) in most studies. D3 is also the form the skin makes.

Why D3 is paired with K2

Vitamin D raises calcium absorption from the gut. Vitamin K is needed to activate proteins such as osteocalcin, which bind calcium into bone. Pairing the two is a common approach, though trials have not shown that the combination prevents fractures. We include K2 because both nutrients contribute to normal bones. We use 55 mcg of K2 as MK-7 (menaquinone-7), the long-acting form of vitamin K2.

Why 600 IU and not 60,000 IU

600 IU a day is the adult Recommended Dietary Allowance (800 IU over age 70), and it is used daily to maintain levels. High-dose sachets such as 60,000 IU are given weekly by doctors to correct a diagnosed deficiency. That is treatment, not daily nutrition (see vitamin D 60,000 IU vs daily 600 IU). The upper limit for adults is 4,000 IU a day. If you have been told you are deficient, follow your doctor's plan.

Best time to take vitamin D3

With a meal that contains some fat, at a consistent time. Breakfast is easiest to remember, which is why D3 + K2 is in the Day Pack.

Who should be careful

  • Warfarin or other vitamin K antagonists: vitamin K can reduce the effect of warfarin. Do not take a product with K2 without your doctor's approval.
  • Steroids, orlistat, some statins and thiazide diuretics can interact with vitamin D. Ask your doctor.
  • High calcium levels, kidney stones or sarcoidosis: ask your doctor first.

FAQ

What is the best time to take vitamin D3?

With a meal that contains some fat, at the same time every day. Breakfast or lunch both work.

Should vitamin D3 be taken with K2?

Many people take them together because vitamin D raises calcium absorption and vitamin K helps activate the proteins that use calcium in bone. Anyone on warfarin must speak to their doctor first.

Is 600 IU of vitamin D enough?

600 IU is the daily recommendation for adults up to 70 and is meant to maintain normal levels. People with a diagnosed deficiency usually need a doctor-prescribed higher dose for a period.

/ingredients/vitamin-b12-methylcobalamin.h1: Vitamin B12: methylcobalamin vs cyanocobalamin, dose and timing
/ingredients/vitamin-b12-methylcobalamin.inner:
Both methylcobalamin and cyanocobalamin raise vitamin B12 levels. Cyanocobalamin is converted in the body, while methylcobalamin is already an active form. B12 can be taken at any time, though many people take it in the morning. The Super Routine Day Pack contains 2.5 mcg of methylcobalamin (100% RDA) as part of its 13 multivitamins.

Who is most at risk of low B12

B12 is found almost only in animal foods, so vegetarians and vegans are at higher risk, and that covers a large share of India. Absorption also falls with age, and with long-term use of metformin or acid-reducing medicines (proton pump inhibitors and H2 blockers). Low B12 can cause tiredness, poor concentration, and tingling in the hands and feet.

What B12 does

Vitamin B12 contributes to normal energy-yielding metabolism, the formation of red blood cells, normal nerve function and the reduction of tiredness and fatigue.

Methylcobalamin vs cyanocobalamin

Honest summary: both work for most healthy people, and there is limited evidence that one is clearly superior. We chose methylcobalamin because it is already active and is widely used in Indian pharmacy B12 products.

Why 2.5 mcg, and when higher doses are used

Super Routine gives 100% of the daily requirement, not a megadose. A daily dose in the low micrograms is meant to maintain normal B12 status in people who absorb it normally, and the intrinsic factor pathway absorbs small doses like this efficiently.

High oral doses (500–1,000 mcg) or injections are used to correct a deficiency, or when absorption is poor, for example in older adults or after long-term metformin or acid-reducing medicines. At those doses only about 1% is absorbed, by passive diffusion. That is treatment and should be guided by your doctor. No upper limit has been set for B12, because excess is excreted.

Best time to take vitamin B12

B12 can be taken at any time, with or without food. We put it in the Day Pack because it supports energy metabolism and fits the morning routine with the other multivitamins, including vitamin D3, and the trace minerals.

Is methylcobalamin better than cyanocobalamin?

Both raise B12 levels. Methylcobalamin is an active form and cyanocobalamin is converted in the body. Evidence that one is clearly better for healthy people is limited.

Any time, with or without food. Many people take it in the morning, which is when it is in the Super Routine Day Pack.

Can I take B12 if I am on metformin?

Metformin can lower B12 levels over time, so B12 is often recommended alongside it. Ask your doctor to check your levels.

/ingredients/zinc-picolinate/.description: Zinc picolinate explained: benefits, why 17 mg, the best time to take zinc, and whether you can take zinc and magnesium together.
/ingredients/zinc-picolinate/.h1: Zinc picolinate: dose, timing and taking it with magnesium
/ingredients/zinc-picolinate/.inner:
Yes, most people can take zinc and magnesium together at normal doses. Very high zinc intakes (around 142 mg a day) can reduce magnesium absorption, so Super Routine keeps them apart anyway: 17 mg of elemental zinc as zinc picolinate in the Day Pack and magnesium in the Night Pack. Take zinc with food if it upsets your stomach.

Our dose17 mg elemental
PackDay

UL40 mg/day

Zinc is one of seven nutrients in the Super Routine Trace Minerals blend in the Day sachet.

What zinc does

Zinc is a co-factor for hundreds of enzymes. It contributes to normal immune function, normal protein and DNA synthesis, normal skin, hair and nails, and normal fertility and reproduction. Diets heavy in cereals and legumes, which are common in India, contain phytates that reduce zinc absorption.

Why picolinate

Zinc picolinate is zinc bound to picolinic acid. A small early study found it raised zinc levels more than gluconate or citrate. The evidence is limited, but picolinate is a well-tolerated chelated form, and much better than poorly absorbed zinc oxide.

Why 17 mg

The ICMR-NIN 2020 RDA for Indian men is 17 mg a day (13 mg for women). It is set higher than the US figure of 11 mg because phytate-rich Indian diets reduce how much zinc is absorbed. 17 mg covers that need while staying below the 40 mg upper limit. Doses of 50 mg or more a day over weeks can lower copper levels, which is why we avoid high-dose zinc and include 1.7 mg of copper in the same trace mineral blend.

Can I take zinc and magnesium together?

At normal supplement doses, yes. The interaction that has been measured involves very high zinc intake (around 142 mg a day), which reduced magnesium absorption. Super Routine still separates them, with zinc in the morning and magnesium glycinate at night, so the two minerals never compete.

Read the full guide: Can you take zinc and magnesium together?

Best time to take zinc

  • Zinc absorbs well on an empty stomach, but it can cause nausea. Taking it after breakfast, as in the Day Pack, is easier on the stomach.
  • Keep it away from iron supplements of 25 mg or more, which reduce zinc absorption.

Who should be careful

  • Antibiotics (quinolones, tetracyclines): take the antibiotic 2 hours before, or 4–6 hours after, zinc.
  • Penicillamine: separate by at least 1 hour.
  • Thiazide diuretics increase zinc loss. Ask your doctor.

FAQ

Can you take zinc and magnesium together?

Yes, at normal doses. Only very high zinc intakes (about 142 mg a day) have been shown to reduce magnesium absorption. Super Routine separates them anyway: zinc in the Day Pack, magnesium in the Night Pack.

What is the best time to take zinc?

After a meal if it upsets your stomach, and away from iron supplements. In Super Routine it is taken after breakfast.

/ingredients/himalayan-shilajit/.inner:
Shilajit is traditionally taken in the morning, after breakfast. Studies have used 250–500 mg of purified resin a day. Human research is early and small. The most important thing is purity: raw shilajit can contain heavy metals, so only purified, third-party-tested shilajit should be used.

Studied dose250 mg purified
In Super RoutineNot included

What shilajit is

Shilajit is a sticky, tar-like resin that seeps from rocks in the Himalayas. It forms over centuries from decomposed plant matter and has been used in Ayurveda for vitality for a very long time. It is rich in fulvic acid, along with compounds called dibenzo-alpha-pyrones and trace minerals.

What the research shows

Human research is limited. In a 2019 trial, recreationally active men took 250 mg or 500 mg of purified shilajit a day for 8 weeks. The higher dose was linked to better retention of muscle strength after a fatiguing exercise test. Other small studies have looked at energy and male hormone levels. These are early findings in small groups, so we describe shilajit as a traditional ingredient that is being studied for energy and stamina, not as a proven treatment.

Shilajit: morning or night?

Traditional use and most brands favour the morning, because shilajit is used for energy and vitality. There is no clinical evidence that one time is better, so consistency matters more. Shilajit is not in the current Super Routine formula. For a morning routine, see what is in the Day Pack now.

Purity: the part that matters most

Raw or poorly processed shilajit can contain lead, arsenic, mercury and cadmium, along with fungal contamination. Look for a specification of no detectable lead, arsenic, mercury, cadmium or thallium, confirmed by an independent laboratory for each batch. To check any brand's report, see how to read a shilajit lab report for heavy metals.

Who should avoid it

  • Pregnant or breastfeeding women, and children.
  • Anyone with a medical condition, or taking any medicine: ask your doctor first.
  • Stop taking it and see a doctor if you notice any unusual symptoms.

Traditionally in the morning, because it is used for energy and vitality. No study shows one time is better.

Human studies have used 250–500 mg a day of purified shilajit. It is not in the current Super Routine formula.

Is shilajit safe?

Only purified, lab-tested shilajit should be used, because raw resin can contain heavy metals. Avoid it if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, and speak to your doctor if you have a medical condition or take medicines.

/science/vitamin-d-60000-iu-vs-daily-600.title: Vitamin D 60,000 IU Weekly vs Daily 600 IU: Which Is Right?
/science/vitamin-d-60000-iu-vs-daily-600.description: Vitamin D3 60,000 IU sachets vs a daily 600 IU dose: what each is for, why 60K weekly averages 8,571 IU a day, blood levels, safety and when to test.
/science/vitamin-d-60000-iu-vs-daily-600.h1: Vitamin D 60,000 IU weekly vs daily 600 IU: which is right for you?
/science/vitamin-d-60000-iu-vs-daily-600.inner:
60,000 IU is a treatment dose, usually taken once a week for 6–12 weeks to correct a measured deficiency. 600 IU a day is the adult maintenance requirement (ICMR-NIN and NIH). A weekly 60,000 IU sachet averages about 8,570 IU a day, over twice the 4,000 IU upper limit, so it is not a long-term dose.

Adult requirement600 IU/day
Adult upper limit4,000 IU/day
60,000 IU weekly≈ 8,571 IU/day
Adequate blood level20 ng/mL or more

Vitamin D3 60,000 IU sachets and capsules are among the most searched supplements in India, and many people take them without a test, often for months. This guide explains what the two doses are for, using the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS), the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (ICMR-NIN) and Indian clinical studies that used the 60,000 IU regimen.

The numbers side by side

DoseWhat it isAverage per day
600 IU daily (15 mcg)Adult requirement (ICMR-NIN 2020; NIH RDA for ages 19–70)600 IU
800 IU daily (20 mcg)NIH RDA for adults over 70800 IU
4,000 IU daily (100 mcg)NIH Tolerable Upper Intake Level for adults4,000 IU
60,000 IU once a monthSometimes used as maintenance after a course, on a doctor's advice≈ 2,000 IU
60,000 IU once a weekShort treatment course for a measured deficiency≈ 8,571 IU

The daily averages are simple arithmetic (60,000 ÷ 7 and 60,000 ÷ 30). 1 mcg of vitamin D equals 40 IU.

What 60,000 IU weekly is used for in India

In Indian clinical studies, 60,000 IU appears as a short course for people whose blood test shows low vitamin D, not as an everyday supplement. Examples:

  • Women with vitamin D below 20 ng/mL received 60,000 IU weekly for 8 weeks in a Jabalpur study.
  • Patients at Tata Memorial Centre with levels of 20 ng/mL or less received 60,000 IU weekly for 8 weeks, followed by 800 IU a day as maintenance.
  • Children with deficiency received 60,000 IU weekly for 6 weeks at BHU Varanasi. Most reached sufficiency, but only 23% of those who did were still sufficient 3 months after stopping. The authors stress the need for regular monitoring and maintenance.

The pattern is consistent: a correction course, a re-test, then a lower maintenance dose. A 60,000 IU sachet every week with no end date is not part of that pattern.

Weekly or daily: does it matter?

Both can raise blood levels. In a 2026 randomised study of 50 vitamin D-deficient adults with long-bone fractures, 60,000 IU weekly for 12 weeks raised blood levels more than 1,000 IU daily (32.8 vs 27.3 ng/mL at 12 weeks), and both were well tolerated. That was a supervised treatment setting with baseline levels below 30 ng/mL.

For healthy people, regular modest doses look sensible. A 2021 meta-analysis of 43 trials found a small overall reduction in acute respiratory infections with vitamin D; the protective effect was seen with daily doses of 400–1,000 IU, although the formal test for a difference between daily and less frequent dosing was not significant. Very large, infrequent doses can backfire: in a trial of 2,256 women aged 70 or older, a single 500,000 IU dose each year increased falls by 15% and fractures by 26% compared with placebo.

How much is too much?

The NIH uses blood 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D) levels to judge status:

Blood 25(OH)DWhat the NIH says
Below 12 ng/mL (30 nmol/L)At risk of deficiency
20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L) or moreGenerally adequate for bone and overall health in healthy people
Above 50 ng/mL (125 nmol/L)Linked to potential adverse effects
Above 150 ng/mL (375 nmol/L)Typical of vitamin D toxicity

Toxicity raises blood calcium. This is not only theoretical in India: at PGIMER Chandigarh, vitamin D intoxication caused 8.7% of the cases of sustained high blood calcium among hospitalised adults.

People also respond differently. In a Delhi study, children with obesity given 60,000 IU weekly for five doses had a 25% smaller rise in blood levels than children of normal weight, while some normal-weight children briefly went above the normal range. This is why the right dose depends on a test, not on a pack size.

Which one should you take?

Your situationUsual approach
Blood test shows deficiencyDoctor-prescribed course (often 60,000 IU weekly for 6–12 weeks), re-test, then maintenance
No test, limited sun, want everyday supportA daily dose around the 600 IU requirement, staying under 4,000 IU a day in total
Already on a 60,000 IU courseDo not add other vitamin D products without asking your doctor
High calcium, kidney stones, sarcoidosis or kidney diseaseOnly under medical supervision

Whatever the dose, take it with a meal: the NIH notes that fat in the gut enhances vitamin D absorption. Orlistat can lower vitamin D absorption, and vitamin D can interact with some statins. For timing details, see the best time to take vitamin D3 and B12.

How the Super Routine Day Pack fits

The Super Routine Day Pack contains vitamin D3 600 IU with K2, taken after breakfast as part of 13 vitamins and 7 trace minerals at 100% RDA. That is a daily maintenance amount that matches the adult requirement, not a treatment for deficiency. If your doctor has prescribed 60,000 IU, finish that course and ask them whether a daily 600 IU afterwards suits you. If you take warfarin, speak to your doctor first because the pack contains vitamin K2. Price and pack details are in the Super Routine FAQ, and the full list of what to take when is in how the two sachets work.

Ask your doctor or pharmacist before starting any vitamin D product if you have a medical condition or take regular medicines.

FAQ

Is 60,000 IU vitamin D safe to take every week?

Only as a short course prescribed after a blood test. Taken weekly it averages about 8,570 IU a day, which is above the 4,000 IU adult upper limit, and long-term use without monitoring can raise blood calcium.

How long should I take vitamin D 60,000 IU?

Indian studies typically used 6 to 12 weeks, followed by a re-test and a lower maintenance dose. Follow your doctor's plan rather than continuing indefinitely.

Is 600 IU of vitamin D a day enough?

600 IU is the daily requirement for most adults (800 IU over 70) and is meant to maintain normal levels. It is not designed to correct a diagnosed deficiency.

Can I take daily vitamin D after a 60,000 IU course?

That is the usual pattern in studies: a correction course followed by a daily maintenance dose. Ask your doctor which dose suits your blood level.

/science/shilajit-lab-report-heavy-metal.title: How to Read a Shilajit Lab Report for Heavy Metals
/science/shilajit-lab-report-heavy-metal.description: Shilajit lab report explained: lead, arsenic, mercury and cadmium limits in ppm, what a real certificate of analysis shows, red flags and accredited testing.
/science/shilajit-lab-report-heavy-metal.h1: How to read a shilajit lab report for heavy metals
/science/shilajit-lab-report-heavy-metal.inner:
A real shilajit lab report (certificate of analysis) names an accredited laboratory, matches your batch number, and gives a measured number in ppm (mg/kg) for lead, arsenic, mercury and cadmium. Limits often cited for herbal products are 10 ppm for lead and arsenic, 1 ppm for mercury and about 0.2–0.3 ppm for cadmium. Lower is better.

Lead, arsenic (herbal limit)10 ppm
Mercury1 ppm
Cadmium≈ 0.2–0.3 ppm
1 ppm equals1 mg per kg

Shilajit is a mineral-rich resin from mountain rock, so it naturally carries whatever metals are in that rock. Many brands now say "lab tested", but a phrase on a label is not a result. This guide shows what a genuine heavy-metal report contains, how to read the numbers, and the red flags that should make you put the jar down.

Why shilajit needs heavy-metal testing

  • A 2024 review in Biological Trace Element Research found around 65 elements reported in shilajit, including toxic metals such as lead, arsenic, cadmium and mercury. Most studies found levels below the permissible limits, but some found them exceeded, and the authors conclude that taking shilajit without knowing its metal levels is not safe.
  • A 2021 analysis of Indian and Pakistani shilajit found lead, arsenic and mercury above permissible limits in the samples tested.
  • The US Department of Defense's Operation Supplement Safety notes that raw shilajit can contain lead, cadmium, arsenic and mercury, and that "without laboratory testing, there is no way to know the actual ingredients."
  • This is not only a shilajit issue. In a 2008 JAMA study, 20.7% of Ayurvedic medicines bought online contained detectable lead, mercury or arsenic, and 75% of those products claimed Good Manufacturing Practices.

The parts of a shilajit lab report

FieldWhat to look for
Laboratory nameAn independent lab, not the brand itself. In India, look for NABL accreditation to ISO/IEC 17025 for the test in question.
Report number and dateRecent, and from before the batch was sold
Sample or batch numberMust match the batch number printed on your pack
MethodAn instrumental method for trace metals such as ICP-MS or ICP-OES
ResultAn actual number for each metal, with units
Limit of quantification (LOQ)The smallest amount the lab can measure. "ND" or "BLQ" means not detected or below that level.
SpecificationThe limit the result is judged against, ideally shown next to it

Reading the numbers

Results are usually in ppm (parts per million, the same as mg/kg) or ppb (parts per billion, µg/kg). 1 ppm = 1,000 ppb. A lead result of 0.5 ppm is the same as 500 ppb.

The 2024 review summarises the levels recommended by the WHO and the US FDA for herbal products:

MetalLimit often cited for herbal productsWhat a good report shows
Lead (Pb)10 ppmA measured value well below the limit, or ND
Arsenic (As)10 ppmA measured value well below the limit, or ND
Mercury (Hg)1 ppmND or a very low value
Cadmium (Cd)0.2–0.3 ppmND or a very low value

These are ceilings, not targets. To see what a result means for you, multiply it by the amount you take. Example: shilajit with 1 ppm lead taken at 250 mg (0.25 g) a day gives 0.25 micrograms of lead a day. Smaller is always better, and no one should treat a "passing" result as permission to take more than the label says.

Red flags on a shilajit lab report

  • No numbers: "heavy metals: complies" or "passed" without a value for each metal.
  • Missing metals: only lead tested, with no arsenic, mercury or cadmium.
  • No batch match: the report is for a different batch, or has no batch number at all.
  • Old or undated: a report from years ago does not describe what is in today's jar.
  • No units, or the wrong ones: a result of "0.8" means nothing without ppm or ppb.
  • In-house only: the brand tested its own product, or the lab cannot be found.
  • Unverifiable accreditation: you can check a lab's status with NABL.

What else a good report covers

Heavy metals are the priority, but a complete certificate usually also shows microbial tests (total plate count, yeast and mould, E. coli, Salmonella) and, for many brands, fulvic acid content. WebMD notes that the FDA has not tested shilajit products to confirm that they contain what their labels state, and that shilajit's contents vary by mountain range, so batch-level testing matters.

Who should avoid shilajit

  • Anyone allergic to shilajit (mineral pitch, mumio). Operation Supplement Safety lists possible allergic reactions, raised blood pressure and dizziness.
  • Pregnant or breastfeeding women: it is not known whether shilajit is safe.
  • People with kidney, liver or prostate problems, or on testosterone therapy: speak to a doctor first.
  • Anyone on regular medicines: interactions between shilajit and medicines are not fully understood.

How Super Routine handles testing

Shilajit is not in the current Super Routine formula. The same principle applies to everything we make: Super Routine is pre-launch, and each batch will be tested by an independent laboratory for identity, content and contaminants, including heavy metals, before release. The reports will be published on this site with the batch number, so you can read them using the checklist above. See what is in the Day Pack and Night Pack now, and the Super Routine FAQ for common questions.

Ask your doctor or pharmacist before taking shilajit if you have a medical condition or take regular medicines.

FAQ

What is a safe level of lead in shilajit?

Limits often cited for herbal products are 10 ppm for lead and arsenic, 1 ppm for mercury and about 0.2 to 0.3 ppm for cadmium. A good report shows values well below these, or not detected.

Is Indian shilajit safe?

It depends on the batch, not the country. Studies of Indian and Pakistani shilajit have found heavy metals above permissible limits in some samples, so only buy purified shilajit with a batch-matched lab report.

What does ND mean on a shilajit lab report?

ND means not detected: the metal was below the smallest amount the lab can measure. Check the report's limit of quantification to see how low that is.

How do I know if a shilajit lab report is real?

Check that it names an independent lab you can verify, matches your batch number, is recent, and gives a number with units for lead, arsenic, mercury and cadmium.

/science/daily-vitamins-for-women-india/.description: Which daily vitamins women in India may need: iron, folic acid, vitamin D, calcium and B12. ICMR-NIN requirements, upper limits, timing and cautions.
/science/daily-vitamins-for-women-india/.h1: Daily vitamins for women in India: what matters most
/science/daily-vitamins-for-women-india/.inner:
For most women in India the nutrients that matter most are iron (needs are highest during the menstruating years), folic acid if you could become pregnant, vitamin D and calcium for bones, and vitamin B12 if you are vegetarian. Test before taking iron, keep iron and calcium apart, and stay under each upper limit.

Iron (ICMR-NIN, women)29 mg/day
Folic acid if pregnancy possible400 mcg/day (NIH)
Calcium (ICMR-NIN)1,000 mg/day
Vitamin D600 IU/day

Search results for "daily vitamins for women" are mostly product listings with 25 or more ingredients. This guide starts from what Indian women actually need, using the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (ICMR-NIN) 2020 requirements for Indians and the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements for upper limits and interactions. Food comes first; supplements fill specific gaps.

Daily needs for adult women in India

NutrientICMR-NIN RDA, women (2020)Adult upper limit (NIH)Who is most likely to fall short
Iron29 mg45 mgHeavy periods, pregnancy, vegetarian diets
Folate220 mcg DFE1,000 mcg (folic acid from supplements and fortified foods)Women who could become pregnant
Calcium1,000 mg2,500 mg (19–50), 2,000 mg (51+)Low dairy intake, after menopause
Vitamin D600 IU4,000 IULittle sun exposure, mostly indoor work
Vitamin B122.2 mcgNone setVegetarians and vegans

The RDAs are totals from food and supplements. ICMR-NIN uses a reference body weight of 55 kg for Indian women. Pregnancy and breastfeeding change these needs; follow your doctor's prenatal advice.

Iron: important, but test first

Women need far more iron than men during the menstruating years: the NIH RDA is 18 mg for women aged 19–50 versus 8 mg for men. The ICMR-NIN requirement for Indian women is higher still, at 29 mg a day. The NIH lists heavy periods and pregnancy as the main risk factors for deficiency, and notes that vegetarian diets need about 1.8 times more iron.

Iron is still not a just-in-case supplement. The upper limit is 45 mg a day, and doses at or above that commonly cause nausea and constipation. People with haemochromatosis should avoid iron supplements. Ask for a blood test (haemoglobin and ferritin) before starting, and take iron only as advised.

  • Vitamin C, for example from lemon, amla or guava, improves absorption of plant iron.
  • Take iron and calcium supplements at different times of day.
  • Levothyroxine (thyroid medicine) should not be taken within 4 hours of iron.
  • Acid-reducing medicines (PPIs) lower iron absorption.

Folic acid: for any woman who could become pregnant

The NIH states that women of childbearing age should get 400 mcg a day of folic acid from supplements or fortified foods, on top of folate from food. The US Preventive Services Task Force advises starting 400–800 mcg a day at least one month before conception and continuing through the first 2–3 months of pregnancy. Keep folic acid from supplements and fortified foods under 1,000 mcg a day unless a doctor prescribes more. If you take antiepileptic medicines or methotrexate, check with your doctor before taking folate.

Vitamin D and calcium: for bones

Vitamin D contributes to normal calcium absorption and bones. The adult requirement is 600 IU a day; stay under 4,000 IU unless a doctor prescribes a treatment course (see vitamin D 60,000 IU vs daily 600 IU).

For calcium, food is the best starting point: dairy foods such as milk, curd and paneer. If you supplement, absorption is highest in doses of 500 mg or less, so split larger amounts. Calcium carbonate is absorbed better with food; calcium citrate can be taken without food. The NIH notes that higher supplemental calcium might increase the risk of kidney stones, and that calcium should be kept 4 hours from levothyroxine and 2 hours from quinolone antibiotics. The NIH RDA rises to 1,200 mg for women over 50.

Vitamin B12: essential for vegetarians

B12 is found naturally in animal foods and is poorly represented in plants, so vegetarian and vegan women are at higher risk of low levels. Dairy and eggs help, but many vegetarians benefit from a supplement. The ICMR-NIN requirement is 2.2 mcg a day.

A simple day and night routine for women

WhenWhatWhy then
Morning, with breakfastVitamin D, B12, folic acidVitamin D absorbs best with a meal containing fat
Midday, with a vitamin C-rich meal (if prescribed)IronKeeps iron away from calcium and thyroid medicine
Evening, with dinnerCalcium (500 mg or less at a time), magnesiumSpaces calcium away from iron

More on which supplements to keep apart is in supplements not to take together.

Pregnancy and breastfeeding

Needs change in pregnancy (the NIH iron RDA rises to 27 mg), and prenatal supplements should be chosen with your doctor. Some popular "women's wellness" herbs are not suitable: the NIH says ashwagandha may not be safe during pregnancy or breastfeeding, and it may affect thyroid function.

How Super Routine fits for women

The Super Routine Day Pack (after breakfast) contains 13 vitamins and 7 trace minerals at 100% RDA, including vitamin D3 600 IU with K2, vitamin B12 2.5 mcg, folate 300 mcg and zinc 17 mg, plus L-theanine 200 mg and Panax ginseng 200 mg. The Night Pack (after dinner) contains magnesium glycinate 2000 mg (280 mg elemental), ashwagandha KSM-66 600 mg and omega-3 deep sea fish oil with 1000 mg EPA + DHA. It covers vitamin D, B12, folate, iodine and magnesium at everyday levels, but it deliberately contains no iron or calcium, so women who need those should take them separately, as advised by their doctor and spaced as above. /science/magnesium-glycinate-and-ashwaga.inner:
Yes, for most healthy adults. NIH fact sheets list no interaction between magnesium and ashwagandha. The cautions come from each one separately: keep supplemental magnesium under 350 mg a day, and avoid ashwagandha if you are pregnant, have thyroid or liver problems, or take sedatives, thyroid, diabetes, blood pressure or immune-suppressing medicines.

Magnesium glycinate and ashwagandha are two of the most popular evening supplements in India, and they are often sold in the same tablet. This guide covers what each one does, whether taking them together is safe, what the only trial of a similar combination found, and how to time them. Every fact here comes from the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS), NCCIH or a peer-reviewed study, listed at the end.

Can you take magnesium glycinate and ashwagandha together?

Yes, for most healthy adults. The NIH ODS fact sheets for magnesium and for ashwagandha each list the medicines they interact with. Neither lists the other. Magnesium's interactions are with certain antibiotics, bisphosphonates, diuretics and acid-reducing medicines; ashwagandha's are with thyroid, diabetes, blood pressure, immunosuppressant and sedative medicines. So the pair has no known interaction of its own, and the safety rules are simply the rules for each ingredient.

Why people take them together

They do different jobs. Magnesium is an essential mineral; it contributes to normal muscle and nervous system function, and many diets fall short of the recommended amount. Ashwagandha is an Ayurvedic herb that has been studied for stress and sleep. The ODS summarises that several small, short trials found it reduced stress and anxiety compared with placebo, and a 2021 meta-analysis of five studies found a small but significant effect on sleep, larger in people with insomnia. Both are commonly taken in the evening as part of a wind-down routine.

What the research on the combination shows

There are no large trials of magnesium glycinate plus ashwagandha specifically. The closest is a 2026 randomised, double-blind trial in 103 healthy, physically active adults. One group took a morning supplement containing 600 mg ashwagandha with another adaptogen; another took an evening supplement with magnesium L-threonate (145 mg magnesium), L-theanine and apigenin; a third took both; a fourth took placebos, for two weeks.

The results were honest and modest. The morning ashwagandha group alone showed lower weekly perceived stress and better subjective sleep quality than placebo. The group taking both did not do better; on sleep quality, the morning-only group did better than the combination group. The authors note that healthy people over a short period may have little room to improve. The magnesium form was threonate, not glycinate, so the result does not transfer directly. The fair conclusion: the combination is not proven to work better than either alone.

Best time to take magnesium glycinate and ashwagandha

  • Magnesium glycinate: any time of day; most people take it with dinner or in the evening.
  • Ashwagandha: the NIH summary does not set a best time, and the 2026 trial above gave it in the morning. Choose one time and keep to it. Because drowsiness is a possible side effect, the evening suits many people.
  • Space magnesium from antibiotics: take tetracycline or quinolone antibiotics at least 2 hours before, or 4–6 hours after, magnesium. Keep oral bisphosphonates 2 hours apart.
  • Taking zinc as well? Very high zinc doses (around 142 mg a day) can interfere with magnesium absorption. Normal doses are fine; see zinc and magnesium together.

Adding melatonin? Read melatonin and magnesium together; it covers the extra drowsiness and driving cautions.

Who should not take ashwagandha with magnesium

  • Pregnant women: some experts advise against ashwagandha in pregnancy, and the French food safety agency ANSES advises against it during pregnancy and breastfeeding.
  • Thyroid conditions or thyroid medicine: ashwagandha might affect thyroid function; cases of thyrotoxicosis that resolved on stopping have been reported.
  • Liver problems: a few cases of liver injury have been reported with ashwagandha.
  • Men with hormone-sensitive prostate cancer: ashwagandha might not be safe, because it may raise testosterone.
  • Anyone on diabetes, blood pressure, immunosuppressant or sedative medicines: ask your doctor first.
  • Kidney disease: the risk of magnesium toxicity rises when kidney function is impaired.

How much is too much?

Add up magnesium from every product. The 350 mg limit counts magnesium from supplements and medicines (including antacids and laxatives), not from food. Loose stools are the usual first sign of too much. Labels often show the compound weight, not the magnesium itself; our guide to elemental magnesium shows how to work it out. For ashwagandha, the NIH notes that benefits in stress trials appeared greater at 500–600 mg a day, and that safety beyond about 3 months is unknown, so review long-term use with your doctor.

/science/elemental-magnesium-explained/.h1: Elemental magnesium explained: how to read magnesium labels in India
/science/elemental-magnesium-explained/.inner:
Elemental magnesium is the weight of the magnesium itself, without the compound it is bound to. "1000 mg magnesium glycinate" gives only about 140 mg elemental magnesium, because glycinate is roughly 14% magnesium. Compare products by elemental magnesium, and keep the total from supplements under 350 mg a day.

Glycinate≈14% magnesium
Citrate≈11–16%
Oxide≈60%, poorly absorbed
Supplement limit350 mg/day elemental

Magnesium never comes alone in a tablet or sachet. It is always bound to something else (glycine, citric acid, oxygen, chloride) to make a stable compound. That compound is what is weighed on many labels, which is why two products that both say "500 mg" can contain very different amounts of magnesium. This guide explains the difference and how to compare products sold in India.

What does elemental magnesium mean?

Elemental magnesium is the share of a compound's weight that is magnesium. The rest is the carrier. The NIH Office of Dietary Supplements notes that a product's Supplement Facts panel declares the amount of elemental magnesium, and ConsumerLab explains that magnesium can make up less than half the weight of compounds such as citrate, chloride and glycinate. Recommended intakes and upper limits are always given in elemental magnesium.

How much elemental magnesium is in each form?

Percentages for oxide, carbonate, hydroxide, chloride, lactate, aspartate, sulfate and gluconate come from a 2019 review in Medical Sciences. For citrate, ConsumerLab gives 11.2% for magnesium citrate and 16.2% for trimagnesium dicitrate, both of which may be labelled "magnesium citrate". The glycinate figure is calculated from its formula: magnesium (24.3 g/mol) is about 14% of magnesium bisglycinate (about 172 g/mol).

More elemental magnesium is not the same as more absorbed

Oxide looks best on paper, with 60% magnesium, but the NIH notes that forms which dissolve well in liquid are absorbed more completely, and that the aspartate, citrate, lactate and chloride forms tend to have higher bioavailability than oxide and sulfate. A small glycinate dose may therefore be a better daily top-up than a large oxide one. Absorption also depends on the dose and on your own magnesium status.

How to read a magnesium label in India

Look for which of these two lines the label uses:

  • "Magnesium glycinate 1000 mg" means the compound. Multiply by the percentage above: about 140 mg of magnesium.
  • "Magnesium (as magnesium glycinate) 140 mg" or "elemental magnesium 140 mg" means the magnesium itself. ConsumerLab explains that a line written this way should contain that amount of actual magnesium.

If a label gives only the compound weight and the brand will not tell you the elemental figure, you cannot compare it fairly with other products. Also check the serving size: a "per serving" figure may mean two or three tablets.

The RDA is your total from food and supplements. The 350 mg upper limit applies only to magnesium from supplements and medicines, not food. A supplement is meant to close the gap between what you eat and what you need, not to supply the whole RDA.

Signs you are taking too much

The NIH says high doses of magnesium from supplements or medicines often cause diarrhoea, which can be accompanied by nausea and abdominal cramping. Very large doses of magnesium-containing laxatives and antacids (typically over 5,000 mg a day) have caused toxicity, and the risk rises with impaired kidney function. Count antacids and laxatives that contain magnesium in your daily total.

Medicines to space from magnesium

  • Tetracycline and quinolone antibiotics (doxycycline, ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin): take at least 2 hours before or 4–6 hours after magnesium.
  • Oral bisphosphonates (alendronate): keep 2 hours apart.
  • Diuretics and long-term proton pump inhibitors: they can change magnesium levels; ask your doctor.

The Super Routine Night Pack contains magnesium glycinate 2000 mg, giving 280 mg elemental magnesium. That is 80% of the 350 mg supplemental limit, so if you also take another magnesium product, or antacids or laxatives that contain magnesium, add the elemental amounts together and keep the total under 350 mg. We chose magnesium glycinate for its gentle profile on the stomach. Zinc is kept in the separate Day Pack (see zinc and magnesium together). FAQ

How much elemental magnesium is in 500 mg of magnesium glycinate?

About 70 mg. Magnesium glycinate is roughly 14% magnesium by weight, so 1000 mg gives about 140 mg.

Is 140 mg of elemental magnesium enough?

It is a top-up, not a full day's need. Indian adults need 370–440 mg a day in total (ICMR-NIN), mostly from food. 140 mg stays well under the 350 mg limit for supplements.

Which form of magnesium has the most elemental magnesium?

Magnesium oxide, at about 60%. But the NIH notes that oxide is absorbed less well than citrate, chloride, lactate or aspartate.

Does the 350 mg limit include magnesium from food?

No. The NIH upper limit of 350 mg covers magnesium from supplements and medicines only. Magnesium from food does not count towards it.

The morning stack

Vitamin D. The NIH lists limited sun exposure, darker skin, older age and obesity among the factors that raise the risk of low vitamin D, and these apply to many office-based men in Indian cities. Take it with breakfast or another meal. Stay under 4,000 IU a day unless a doctor prescribes a treatment course; excess raises blood calcium and can cause nausea, weakness, excessive thirst and kidney stones. See the best time to take vitamin D3 and B12.

Vitamin B12. B12 comes naturally only from animal foods, so vegetarian men are at higher risk, as are men taking metformin or acid-reducing medicines. Oral absorption of large doses is low (about 1.3% of a 1,000 mcg dose), which is why supplements contain far more than the 2.2 mcg RDA. No upper limit has been set.

Zinc. Zinc contributes to normal immune function. Men need more than women (17 mg vs 13 mg a day per ICMR-NIN), and vegetarians absorb less because of phytates. Keep total zinc under 40 mg a day: about 50 mg or more for weeks can lower copper status. Take quinolone or tetracycline antibiotics at least 2 hours before or 4–6 hours after zinc.

The evening stack

Magnesium. It contributes to normal muscle and nervous system function. Keep supplemental magnesium under 350 mg a day of elemental magnesium; high doses cause diarrhoea. Read the label carefully, because the compound weight is not the magnesium content (see elemental magnesium explained).

Omega-3. There is no RDA for EPA and DHA. For men who rarely eat fish, a fish oil (or an algal oil, for vegetarians, which usually gives 100–300 mg DHA) is one option. Take it with a meal to reduce fishy aftertaste. Men on warfarin should have their INR monitored, and very high doses (4 g a day for years) slightly increased atrial fibrillation risk in people with heart disease.

Optional: ashwagandha or melatonin for sleep and stress. Evidence for ashwagandha on stress and sleep is modest and short-term, and NCCIH notes that guidelines do not recommend melatonin for chronic insomnia. If you try either, see magnesium glycinate and ashwagandha together and the best supplements to take at night.

What men usually do not need

  • Iron: it is not a just-in-case supplement. The adult upper limit is 45 mg a day, and iron interacts with zinc, levothyroxine and levodopa. Take it only if a blood test shows a need.
  • Stacks of single products that overlap: a men's multivitamin plus separate zinc and vitamin D can push you over the limits above. Add up every label.
  • "Booster" claims: be wary of any product that promises hormonal or performance results. Supplements support normal nutrition; they are not medicines.

  • Prostate: the NIH says ashwagandha might not be safe for men with hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, because it may raise testosterone. WebMD advises men with prostate problems, or on testosterone therapy, to talk to a doctor before taking shilajit.
  • Thyroid, diabetes and blood pressure medicines: ashwagandha may interact with them.
  • Melatonin: people with epilepsy and those on blood thinners need medical supervision. Do not drive after taking it.

How to choose daily supplements

  1. Look at your diet first. Vegetarian? Little dairy? Rarely in the sun? Those answers point to specific nutrients.
  2. Test before you take iron or high-dose vitamin D. Both can cause harm in excess.
  3. Add up every product. The NIH warns that people who combine a multivitamin with other supplements and fortified foods can exceed upper limits.
  4. Pick products that print exact doses, so you can check them against the limits above.

1. Vitamin D

ICMR-NIN sets the adult requirement at 600 IU a day. The NIH lists people with limited sun exposure, darker skin and older adults among those most likely to be low. Take it with a meal that contains some fat. Keep total intake under 4,000 IU a day unless your doctor prescribes a treatment dose; excess raises blood calcium and can cause nausea, weakness and kidney stones. Timing is covered in the best time to take vitamin D3 and B12.

2. Vitamin B12

B12 occurs naturally only in animal foods, so vegetarians have a higher risk of deficiency, says the NIH. People over 50 are advised to get B12 mainly from fortified foods or supplements, and metformin and acid-reducing medicines can lower B12 levels. The ICMR-NIN requirement is 2.2 mcg a day; supplements contain far more because only a small fraction of a large oral dose is absorbed. No upper limit has been set.

3. Folic acid (for women who could become pregnant)

The CDC recommends that all women capable of becoming pregnant get 400 mcg of folic acid daily, because taking it before and in early pregnancy lowers the chance of neural tube defects. If you are planning a pregnancy, talk to your doctor about a prenatal supplement.

4. Iron (only if you need it)

Women with heavy periods, pregnant women and vegetarians are more likely to run short of iron, according to the NIH. But iron is not a "take it just in case" supplement. The adult upper limit is 45 mg a day, high doses cause constipation and nausea, and accidental iron overdose is a leading cause of fatal poisoning in children under 6, so store it out of reach. Iron reduces absorption of levothyroxine, and calcium may reduce iron absorption, so take them at different times. Vitamin C improves absorption of iron from plant foods.

5. Calcium (if your diet is low in dairy)

ICMR-NIN sets the adult requirement at 1,000 mg a day. If you eat milk, curd, paneer or ragi daily, you may not need a supplement. If you do, the NIH says absorption is best in doses of 500 mg or less, so split larger amounts, and take calcium carbonate with food. Keep calcium carbonate 4 hours away from levothyroxine.

6. Omega-3 (if you rarely eat fish)

There is no official requirement for EPA and DHA, the omega-3s in fish. If you eat little fish, a fish oil or, for vegetarians, an algal oil supplement is one option; the NIH notes algal oils usually provide about 100–300 mg of DHA. Side effects are usually mild (fishy taste, heartburn). People on warfarin should have their INR monitored.

Do you need a daily multivitamin?

For healthy adults, the evidence is modest. The NIH summarises the US Preventive Services Task Force view: there is insufficient evidence to judge the balance of benefits and harms of multivitamins for preventing heart disease or cancer. A multivitamin can still be a convenient way to fill gaps, especially for vegetarians and older adults, but check that it does not double up on vitamin D, zinc or iron you already take. Men can see our guide to daily supplements for men in India, and women our guide to daily vitamins for women in India. For the most common morning nutrients and how to space them, see the best supplements to take in the morning.

The Night Pack (after dinner) contains magnesium glycinate 2000 mg (280 mg elemental), ashwagandha KSM-66 600 mg and omega-3 deep sea fish oil with 1000 mg EPA + DHA.

To be clear about what it does not cover: there is no iron or calcium, because those depend on individual needs and interact with other nutrients and medicines. The Day Pack includes folate at 100% RDA, but women planning a pregnancy should use a prenatal supplement chosen with their doctor, not Super Routine; it contains ashwagandha and Panax ginseng, which experts advise against in pregnancy. Because the Day Pack is already a multivitamin and mineral, do not add another multivitamin. If you need only one or two nutrients, single products may suit you better; we compare costs openly in Super Routine vs separate supplements. Vitamin D3 and B12 are two of the supplements Indian adults are most often advised to take, and they are commonly prescribed together. Their timing rules are different, though: one depends on food, the other does not. This guide explains both, using the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS), the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (ICMR-NIN) and published research.

Vitamin D3 and B12 timing at a glance

Vitamin D3Vitamin B12

Best timeWith a meal that contains fatAny time that suits your routine
Needs food?Yes, absorption is better with fatNo; supplement B12 is already in free form

Best time to take vitamin D3: with your meal, not on an empty stomach

Vitamin D is fat-soluble. The NIH states that the presence of fat in the gut enhances vitamin D absorption, although some is absorbed without it. So the rule is about the meal, not the clock: take vitamin D3 with breakfast, lunch or dinner, as long as the meal contains some fat (milk, curd, eggs, nuts, ghee or oil in cooking).

One often-quoted study supports taking it with your largest meal. In 2010, Mulligan and Licata asked 17 patients at a US bone clinic, who were not responding to vitamin D treatment, to take their usual dose with the largest meal of the day. After 2–3 months their blood vitamin D levels were on average about 50% higher. It was a small study without a control group, so treat it as a useful hint rather than proof, but it fits the fat-absorption mechanism.

In practice, the best meal is the one you eat every day. For many people that is breakfast, which makes the dose easy to remember.

Best time to take vitamin B12: whenever you will remember it

B12 in food is bound to protein and needs stomach acid to release it. The NIH explains that B12 in supplements is already in free form, so it does not need that step, which means you can take a B12 supplement with or without food. The NIH fact sheet does not recommend any time of day.

The morning is popular simply because it is easy to build into a routine. Large oral doses are standard because absorption through the normal route is limited: the NIH says only about 2% of a 500 mcg dose and 1.3% of a 1,000 mcg dose is absorbed, since the intrinsic factor pathway is saturated at about 1–2 mcg. No upper limit has been set. The NIH also states there is no evidence that absorption differs between supplement forms such as methylcobalamin and cyanocobalamin.

Can you take vitamin D3 and B12 together?

Yes. The NIH fact sheets for vitamin D and vitamin B12 list no interaction between them, and they are absorbed by different routes. Taking them together after breakfast covers both rules: the meal helps vitamin D, and B12 does not mind either way. Combining them also means one habit instead of two, which matters more for results than the exact hour.

Morning or night?

For both vitamins, the evidence we found is about food, not time of day. If your main meal is dinner, taking vitamin D3 then is fine. The one practical reason to prefer the morning is consistency: a breakfast routine is easier to keep than a late-night one.

Who needs to be careful

  • Vitamin D: keep total intake under 4,000 IU a day unless a doctor prescribes more. Too much raises blood calcium, which can cause nausea, vomiting, muscle weakness and kidney stones. Orlistat, statins, steroids and thiazide diuretics interact with vitamin D. If you were prescribed a weekly high-dose sachet, follow your doctor's schedule.
  • Vitamin K2 with D3: no upper limit is set for vitamin K, but it can interact seriously with warfarin. Anyone on warfarin should not start K2 without their doctor.
  • Vitamin B12: metformin and proton pump inhibitors can lower B12 levels. Vegetarians and older adults are at higher risk of low B12, because natural sources are animal foods and absorption from food falls with age.

If you think you may be low in either vitamin, ask your doctor for a blood test rather than guessing a dose.

/science/melatonin-and-magnesium-togethe.inner:
Yes, most healthy adults can take melatonin and magnesium together: the NIH fact sheets list no interaction between them, and they work differently. Melatonin signals night to your body clock; magnesium supports normal nerve and muscle function. Keep supplemental magnesium under 350 mg a day, take melatonin 30–60 minutes before bed, and do not drive afterwards.

Interaction between themNone listed by NIH

Melatonin timing30–60 min before bed
After takingNo driving for 5 hours

Melatonin and magnesium are two of the most common evening supplements, and many sleep products combine them. This guide explains what each one does, what the research on the pair shows (less than marketing suggests), and how to take them safely. It draws on the NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH), the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS), Mayo Clinic and published trials.

Melatonin vs magnesium: how they differ

MelatoninMagnesium
What it isA hormone the brain makes in response to darknessAn essential mineral needed by hundreds of enzymes
What it does for sleepSignals night to the body clock; best studied for sleep timing and jet lagSupports normal nerve and muscle function; sleep evidence is mixed
Daily limitNo official limit; long-term safety data are lacking350 mg/day from supplements (adults)
Common side effectsHeadache, dizziness, nausea, sleepinessDiarrhoea, nausea, cramping at high doses
Main cautionsEpilepsy, blood thinners, dementia, pregnancyKidney disease, some antibiotics, bisphosphonates

Is it safe to take melatonin and magnesium together?

For most healthy adults, yes. The NIH fact sheets on magnesium and melatonin do not list an interaction between the two, and they act on different systems. The risks of the pair are the risks of each one on its own, so the safety rules below still apply.

The bigger risk is doubling up. Many "sleep blends" already contain melatonin, and some antacids and laxatives contain magnesium. Check every label so you are not taking two melatonin products, and count all supplemental magnesium towards the 350 mg limit. See supplements not to take together.

What the research shows for sleep

Melatonin

The NCCIH says there is not enough strong evidence to recommend melatonin for chronic insomnia. It is better supported for sleep timing: in people with delayed sleep-wake phase disorder, a 2016 review found melatonin shortened the time to fall asleep by about 22 minutes compared with placebo. Reviews also found it may reduce jet lag symptoms after eastward flights. Short-term use appears safe for most people; long-term safety is not known.

Magnesium

The evidence for magnesium alone is weaker. A 2026 systematic review of 12 randomised trials found inconsistent results and rated the certainty of evidence low to very low. Its conclusion: current evidence does not support oral magnesium as a routine treatment for insomnia, though some adults may notice modest benefits. The American Cancer Society likewise describes the results as mixed, and notes that magnesium glycinate is a common choice because it is easily absorbed and gentle on the stomach.

Melatonin and magnesium together

We found one placebo-controlled trial of the combination. In 2011, Rondanelli and colleagues gave 43 long-term care residents in Italy (average age about 78) with primary insomnia either a supplement of 5 mg melatonin, 225 mg magnesium and 11.25 mg zinc, or placebo, one hour before bed for 8 weeks. The supplement group had better sleep quality scores and longer total sleep time.

The limits matter. It was a small study in older adults in care, the supplement also contained zinc, and the design cannot show how much each ingredient contributed. It suggests the combination is reasonable to study further; it does not prove that the pair works better than melatonin alone for younger adults.

How to take melatonin and magnesium together

  • Magnesium: take it with dinner or in the evening. A meal reduces stomach upset. Glycinate and other chelated forms are less likely to loosen stools than oxide.
  • Melatonin: take it 30–60 minutes before your planned bedtime. The Rondanelli trial used one hour before bed.
  • Keep the dose modest. Mayo Clinic notes that over-the-counter products vary widely in how much melatonin they contain; the NCCIH reports that a 2017 study found most of 31 products did not match their label. Choose a product that states an exact dose.
  • Do not drive or use machinery within five hours of taking melatonin (Mayo Clinic).
  • Use both alongside good sleep habits: a regular wake time, a dark room and less screen time late at night.

Who should not take melatonin and magnesium together

  • Pregnant or breastfeeding women: melatonin has not been well studied in pregnancy or breastfeeding.
  • People with epilepsy or taking blood thinners: the NCCIH says they need medical supervision to take melatonin.
  • People with dementia: the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends against melatonin for them.
  • People taking diabetes, blood pressure, seizure or immunosuppressant medicines, or birth control pills: Mayo Clinic lists these as possible melatonin interactions.
  • People with kidney disease: the risk of magnesium build-up is higher when the kidneys clear it less well.
  • Antibiotics and bone medicines: take tetracyclines or quinolones (such as doxycycline or ciprofloxacin) at least 2 hours before or 4–6 hours after magnesium, and keep bisphosphonates such as alendronate 2 hours apart from it.

Persistent trouble sleeping deserves a doctor's visit. Supplements are not a substitute for diagnosing the cause.

If you choose to take a melatonin product alongside it, the rules above apply: one clearly labelled product, 30–60 minutes before bed, and no driving afterwards. The sachet also contains ashwagandha, which the NIH notes can cause drowsiness and may interact with sedatives, thyroid, diabetes and blood pressure medicines, so ask your doctor before combining it with melatonin if you take any of these. Zinc is in the separate Day Pack, taken after breakfast, so the minerals are not taken together (see zinc and magnesium together). FAQ

Can I take magnesium and melatonin together every night?

Many adults do, and the NIH lists no interaction between them. Melatonin appears safe short term, but long-term safety is not known, so if you need help sleeping for more than a few weeks, see a doctor.

Which is better for sleep, melatonin or magnesium?

They do different things. Melatonin has better evidence for sleep timing and jet lag; evidence for magnesium is mixed and of low certainty. Neither is recommended as a routine treatment for chronic insomnia.

When should I take magnesium and melatonin?

Take magnesium with dinner or in the evening, and melatonin 30 to 60 minutes before bed. Do not drive or use machinery within five hours of melatonin.

Can I take magnesium glycinate, melatonin and ashwagandha together?

They are often combined in the evening, but ashwagandha and melatonin can both cause drowsiness. Avoid alcohol and sedatives with them, and ask your doctor first if you take any regular medicine or are pregnant.

/science/best-supplements-to-take-in-the.inner:
The best supplements for the day are the ones you actually need, taken with breakfast: vitamin D (fat in the meal helps absorption), vitamin B12 (important for vegetarians and older adults), and zinc or iron if your diet or doctor calls for them, with food to limit nausea. Keep iron apart from calcium, and leave melatonin for bedtime.

Most lists of the "best supplements to take in the morning" are shopping lists. This guide asks which nutrients commonly fall short in Indian diets, and which of those are best taken with breakfast. The answers come from the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (ICMR-NIN) and the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS). Food comes first; a supplement only fills a gap.

Best supplements for the day at a glance

SupplementWhy the morning worksIndian adult RDA (ICMR-NIN 2020)Main caution
Vitamin D3Fat-soluble; fat in the meal enhances absorption600 IUUpper limit 4,000 IU/day; statins, orlistat
Vitamin K2Fat-soluble; absorbed with dietary fatNo Indian RDA listed in the brief note; US AI 90–120 mcgWarfarin
