The RDA figures above are the totals you need from food and supplements combined, not the dose a supplement should contain.

1. Vitamin D: best with a breakfast that contains some fat

For the full timing rules, including whether to combine it with B12, see the best time to take vitamin D3 and B12.

Vitamin D needs a meal, and breakfast is the most regular one. The NIH fact sheet states that the presence of fat in the gut enhances vitamin D absorption, although some is absorbed without it. ICMR-NIN sets the adult requirement at 600 IU a day, the same figure the NIH uses for adults up to 70 (800 IU over 70).

The NIH lists people with darker skin, those who spend little time in the sun and older adults among the groups most at risk of low vitamin D. The adult upper limit is 4,000 IU a day, and too much can raise blood calcium, with nausea, weakness and kidney stones. High vitamin D intakes may also reduce the effect of atorvastatin, lovastatin and simvastatin, and orlistat can lower vitamin D absorption. If your doctor prescribed a weekly high-dose sachet, follow that plan instead.

2. Vitamin K2: a natural partner for vitamin D

Vitamin K is also fat-soluble and is absorbed in the small intestine with dietary fat, so it suits the same breakfast. The NIH notes that MK-7, the form found in natto, is well absorbed and has a longer half-life than vitamin K1. No upper limit has been set because of its low potential for toxicity. The one serious warning is warfarin: people taking it need a consistent vitamin K intake, so do not start K2 without your doctor's agreement.

3. Vitamin B12: the vegetarian essential

B12 is found naturally only in animal foods, and the NIH says vegetarians who avoid meat have a higher risk of deficiency. Older adults are also at risk, because atrophic gastritis, which reduces B12 absorption from food, affects 8% to 9% of adults aged 65 and over. Long-term use of metformin, proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole, or H2 blockers can lower B12 levels too.

Time of day is not critical for B12; the morning is simply easy to remember. Absorption of large oral doses is low (about 2% at 500 mcg, says the NIH), which is why supplements contain far more than the 2.2 mcg RDA; no upper limit has been set. The NIH also states there is no evidence that absorption differs between methylcobalamin and cyanocobalamin. See our vitamin B12 guide.

4. Zinc: after breakfast, never on an empty stomach

Zinc can cause nausea, which is why most people take it after a meal. Absorption from food varies widely, from about 5% to over 50%, depending on phytates, compounds in whole grains and legumes that bind zinc. The NIH notes that vegetarians usually have lower zinc intakes and levels, relevant to many Indian diets built on dal, roti and rice. The NIH suggests soaking beans, grains and seeds before cooking and eating fermented foods, such as idli and dosa batter, to improve zinc absorption.

Keep total zinc under 40 mg a day; 50 mg or more for weeks can lower copper levels. Take quinolone or tetracycline antibiotics at least 2 hours before or 4–6 hours after zinc, and keep iron tablets of 25 mg or more away from it. More in our zinc picolinate guide.

5. Iron: only if you need it, and timed carefully

Take iron only if a doctor or blood test says you need it. The NIH says taking iron with food can reduce side effects such as nausea and constipation, which are more likely at 45 mg a day or more. Vitamin C enhances absorption of plant (non-heme) iron, while phytates and some plant polyphenols reduce it.

  • Do not take iron within 4 hours of levothyroxine (thyroid medicine), which many people take first thing in the morning.
  • Take calcium and iron at different times of day.
  • Keep iron supplements locked away from children: accidental iron overdose is a leading cause of fatal poisoning in children under 6.

6. Calcium: split it, and match the form to the meal

Calcium absorbs best in doses of 500 mg or less, so a 1,000 mg daily target is better split between breakfast and dinner. Calcium carbonate should be taken with a meal; calcium citrate can be taken with or without food. Levothyroxine should not be taken within 4 hours of calcium carbonate, and quinolone antibiotics need 2 hours either side.

What about a multivitamin, omega-3 and ashwagandha?

  • Multivitamin: many contain fat-soluble vitamins and minerals, so breakfast is a sensible time. Check that it does not double up on vitamin D, zinc or iron you already take.
  • Ashwagandha: drowsiness is a reported side effect, which is one reason many people take it in the evening. It should be avoided in pregnancy and may interact with thyroid, diabetes, blood pressure and sedative medicines.

What not to take in the morning

Melatonin. It signals night to your body clock, can cause daytime drowsiness, and Mayo Clinic advises not driving or using machinery within five hours of taking it. It belongs at bedtime; see our guide to the best supplements to take at night. Magnesium can be taken at any time, but many people keep it for the evening, and keeping it apart from zinc removes any question of competition (see zinc and magnesium together).

Which vitamins should I take in the morning?

Doses: reading labels the right way

The other cost of separate supplements is organisation.   • Your doctor prescribed a different dose, such as a weekly high-dose vitamin D sachet, high-dose B12 or iron.
  • You cannot take one of our ingredients, for example ashwagandha or ginseng because of pregnancy or a thyroid condition, or vitamin K because you take warfarin.
  • You are vegetarian and want no fish oil. Our omega-3 is from fish; algal oil is the vegetarian alternative.

"Day and night supplements" simply means splitting a supplement routine by time of day, because a few nutrients work better, or are easier to take, at a particular time. Most of the evidence is about practical things: taking fat-soluble vitamins with a meal, keeping calming ingredients for the evening, and spacing nutrients that can compete. This page explains how the Super Routine day and night sachets apply those rules, and where timing matters less than marketing suggests.

Why the Day sachet goes after breakfast

Fat-soluble vitamins need a meal. According to the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, fat in the gut enhances vitamin D absorption, and vitamin K is absorbed along with dietary fat; the same is true of vitamins A and E. Breakfast is the most regular meal for most people, which makes the routine easy to keep. Our 600 IU of vitamin D3 matches the ICMR-NIN adult requirement and is well below the 4,000 IU upper limit.

Minerals are easier on a full stomach. Nausea is a known effect of zinc on an empty stomach. Our 17 mg of zinc is under the 40 mg upper limit, and copper is included to keep the two in balance.

L-theanine and ginseng suit the day. Both are studied for focus, mental performance and fatigue, and neither contains caffeine. Ginseng can disturb sleep in some people, which is another reason it is not in the Night sachet.

Why the Night sachet goes after dinner

Ashwagandha fits the evening. The NIH summarises a 2021 meta-analysis of five studies (372 adults) that found a small but significant benefit for sleep at 250–600 mg a day over 6–12 weeks, with larger effects at 600 mg. Drowsiness is one of its reported side effects. Our 600 mg matches the dose with the larger effects.

Magnesium and omega-3 are flexible. The NIH does not tie magnesium absorption to time of day, and omega-3 can be taken whenever suits you. We put them in the Night sachet because dinner is usually the largest meal, fish oil absorbs best with food, and it keeps magnesium away from the morning zinc.

The Night sachet contains no melatonin and no sedatives.

Why zinc and magnesium are in different sachets

To be accurate: at normal doses most people can take zinc and magnesium together. The interaction the NIH describes involves very high zinc intakes of about 142 mg a day, far above our 17 mg. We split them anyway because minerals are absorbed in the same part of the gut, and putting them in different sachets removes the question completely. Who should not take Super Routine day and night supplements

  • Anyone pregnant or breastfeeding, or under 18.
  • People taking warfarin or other blood thinners: vitamin K changes warfarin's effect, and omega-3 and ginseng may affect clotting.
  • People taking thyroid medicine or with a thyroid condition: iodine, selenium and ashwagandha can affect thyroid hormones.
  • People taking diabetes or blood pressure medicines, sedatives, MAOI antidepressants or immunosuppressants: ginseng, chromium and ashwagandha may interact with them.
  • People on statins (high vitamin D intakes may reduce the effect of some) or quinolone and tetracycline antibiotics (take them at least 2 hours before or 4–6 hours after either sachet).

The Day sachet already works as a complete multivitamin and mineral at 100% RDA, so do not add another one. What a once-a-day multivitamin cannot do is place calming ingredients in the evening or keep zinc and magnesium apart, and most do not contain omega-3, ashwagandha, L-theanine or ginseng. It may contain nutrients we leave out, such as iron and calcium. If you are comparing costs and doses, read Super Routine vs separate supplements. /science/best-supplements-for-night/.inner:
The best-supported supplements to take at night are melatonin (for jet lag and a late body clock), ashwagandha (small benefits for sleep quality in trials), L-theanine and magnesium (limited but promising evidence). Valerian and chamomile have weak evidence, and kava carries a liver risk. Start with sleep habits; supplements are a support, not a fix.

Strongest evidenceMelatonin (jet lag, late body clock)
AvoidKava (liver injury reports)
Mg upper limit350 mg/day (supplements)
First-line for insomniaCBT-I, not supplements

Search "best supplements for night" and you will find shopping lists. This guide is different: it ranks the common night-time supplements by what the research actually shows, using the NIH's National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH), the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements and recent meta-analyses. Some popular options do well. Some do not. One is a safety concern.

A quick word first. If you have had trouble sleeping for months, the recommended first step is not a supplement. NCCIH notes that the American College of Physicians strongly recommends cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) as the initial treatment for chronic insomnia. A consistent bedtime, a dark room and fewer late screens help any supplement work better.

Best supplements to take at night: the evidence at a glance

SupplementWhat the evidence saysTypical studied doseMain caution
MelatoninHelps jet lag and a delayed body clock; weak for chronic insomniaCommon adult dose 0.5–3 mg, 1 hour or less before bedEpilepsy, blood thinners, pregnancy, dementia
AshwagandhaSmall but significant benefit for sleep in a meta-analysis250–600 mg/day root extract, 6–12 weeksPregnancy, thyroid medicine, liver problems
L-theanineSmall improvements in self-reported sleep quality and sleep onsetVaries by studyFew studies on pure L-theanine
MagnesiumVery little, low-quality research; may help sleep onset in older adultsStay under 350 mg/day from supplementsKidney disease, some antibiotics
ValerianInconsistent trial results; benefit not shownVariesLong-term safety uncertain
ChamomileNo conclusive trial evidenceUsually as teaRagweed allergy
KavaVery little research for sleepNot recommendedLinked to serious liver injury

1. Melatonin: best for jet lag and a late body clock

Melatonin is the hormone that tells your body clock it is night. It is the most studied night-time supplement, but what it helps with is specific.

  • Delayed sleep timing: in a 2018 trial of 307 people cited by NCCIH, melatonin taken 1 hour before a set bedtime helped people fall asleep about 34 minutes earlier.
  • Jet lag: research suggests it may help, from small studies of eastward and westward travel.
  • Chronic insomnia: NCCIH says there is not enough strong evidence, and sleep medicine guidelines have recommended against it for that use.

Short-term use appears to be safe for most people; long-term safety is not established. Mild side effects include headache, dizziness, nausea and sleepiness. People with epilepsy and those taking blood thinners need medical supervision, guidelines recommend against it in dementia, and there is little safety research in pregnancy or breastfeeding. Melatonin may stay active longer in older people and cause daytime drowsiness.

Label accuracy matters too. NCCIH reports that in a 2023 study, 22 of 25 melatonin gummies were inaccurately labelled, with 74% to 347% of the stated amount. Choose one clearly labelled product and never stack two.

2. Ashwagandha: modest benefit after several weeks

According to the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, a 2021 meta-analysis of 5 studies (372 adults) found a small but significant benefit of ashwagandha over placebo for sleep. Doses were 250–600 mg a day of KSM-66 root extract (or 120 mg of another extract) for 6–12 weeks. Benefits were greater at 600 mg a day, with at least 8 weeks of use, and in people with insomnia.

It appears well tolerated for up to about 3 months; long-term safety is unknown. Avoid it in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Rare liver injury has been reported, small studies found changes in thyroid hormone levels, and it may interact with thyroid medicine, sedatives, diabetes and blood pressure medicines, and immunosuppressants. More in our ashwagandha KSM-66 guide.

3. L-theanine: calm without sedation

L-theanine is an amino acid found in tea. A 2025 meta-analysis in Sleep Medicine Reviews (19 articles, 897 participants) found it improved self-reported time to fall asleep, daytime dysfunction and overall sleep quality, though the effects were small and the authors noted a lack of studies on pure L-theanine. Promising, not proven.

4. Magnesium: useful nutrient, unproven sleep aid

Magnesium is often sold as a sleep supplement, but NCCIH says very little research exists: one review suggested it may help sleep onset in older adults, from low-quality studies, and another found conflicting results. Where magnesium earns its place is as a nutrient. Adults need 310–420 mg a day from food and supplements combined, and many people take it in the evening simply because it fits a wind-down routine.

Keep supplemental magnesium under 350 mg a day; high doses often cause diarrhoea. Take tetracycline or quinolone antibiotics at least 2 hours before or 4–6 hours after magnesium, and separate bisphosphonates by 2 hours. People with kidney problems should not take it without medical advice. The glycinate form is gentle on the stomach; see magnesium glycinate explained. Thinking of combining it with melatonin? Read melatonin and magnesium together for sleep.

5. Valerian, chamomile and lavender

These are traditional favourites with thin evidence. NCCIH says valerian trial results are inconsistent and its value for insomnia has not been shown. Chamomile has no conclusive trial evidence, and people allergic to ragweed may react to it. Lavender aromatherapy improved sleep quality in a review of 16 studies, but larger, more rigorous trials are needed. A cup of chamomile tea as part of a routine is fine; just do not expect it to do much on its own.

Night supplements to avoid or use with care

  • Kava: NCCIH says it has been linked to liver injury that is sometimes serious or even fatal. We do not recommend it.
  • L-tryptophan and 5-HTP: data for insomnia are very limited, and L-tryptophan may cause serotonin toxicity with medicines that affect serotonin, such as some antidepressants.
  • CBD: there is insufficient evidence for any sleep disorder, and it can cause liver injury and drug interactions.
  • Multiple "sleep blends" at once: many contain melatonin, so doses add up. See supplements not to take together.

Best vitamins to take before bed (that are not sleep aids)

Not every night-time supplement is about sleep. Omega-3 (EPA and DHA) is a component of every cell membrane and can be taken at any time; taking it with dinner fits many routines. Its usual side effects are mild, such as an unpleasant taste or heartburn, but high doses may cause bleeding problems with warfarin or other anticoagulants, so tell your doctor if you take one.

How the Super Routine Night Pack fits

We built the Night Pack from the evening options with the most sensible evidence and safety profile, at clearly labelled doses, in one sachet taken after dinner:

/science/supplements-not-to-take-togethe.description: A list of 7 supplement combinations to separate or avoid, with spacing times, upper limits and the medicines that interact with minerals.
/science/supplements-not-to-take-togethe.h1: 7 supplements you should not take together
/science/supplements-not-to-take-togethe.inner:
The main combinations to separate or avoid are calcium with iron, iron with zinc, high-dose zinc with copper or magnesium, melatonin with other sleep products, omega-3 or vitamin K with blood thinners, and two products with the same nutrient. Most can still be taken on the same day if you space them a few hours apart.

Most common clashCalcium + iron
Zinc upper limit40 mg/day
Mg upper limit350 mg/day (supplements)
Vitamin D upper limit4,000 IU/day

"Not together" rarely means "never". For most of the pairs below the problem is competition for absorption in the gut, which you solve by taking them at different times of day. A few are about safety, where the answer is to talk to your doctor first. Here is each combination, why it matters and what to do.

Quick reference: which supplements not to take together

CombinationWhyWhat to do
1. Calcium + ironCalcium might reduce iron absorptionTake at different times of day
2. Iron (25 mg+) + zincIron reduces zinc absorptionTake at different times of day
3. High-dose zinc + copper status50 mg+ zinc for weeks inhibits copper absorptionKeep zinc under 40 mg a day
4. Very high-dose zinc + magnesium142 mg zinc a day might reduce magnesium absorptionNormal doses are fine; splitting is optional
5. Melatonin + other sleep productsStacked doses, uncertain label contentUse one melatonin product only
6. Omega-3 or vitamin K + blood thinnersCan change clotting tests (INR)Only with your doctor's agreement
7. Two products with the same nutrientCan push you over the upper limitAdd up every label

1. Calcium and iron

This is the pairing most people have heard of. The NIH Office of Dietary Supplements says calcium might interfere with iron absorption, although the effect has not been definitively established, and experts suggest taking individual calcium and iron supplements at different times of the day. A simple routine is iron in the morning and calcium with dinner, or the other way round.

Calcium absorbs best in small amounts: absorption from supplements is highest at doses of 500 mg or less. If you take more, split it across meals rather than taking it all at once.

2. Iron and zinc

Iron tablets of 25 mg of elemental iron or more, taken at the same time as zinc, can reduce zinc absorption. The iron added to fortified foods does not have a significant effect. If you have been prescribed iron, take it at a different time from any zinc supplement. With Super Routine, that means taking your iron away from the Day Pack, which contains 17 mg of zinc.

3. High-dose zinc and copper

Zinc and copper share an absorption pathway. Doses of 50 mg of zinc or more over a period of weeks can inhibit copper absorption and lead to low copper status. This is one reason the adult upper limit for zinc is 40 mg a day. Long courses of high-dose "immunity" zinc are the usual way people get there. Stay under 40 mg a day from all supplements combined unless a doctor has prescribed more.

4. Very high-dose zinc and magnesium

Very high zinc intakes from supplements, around 142 mg a day, might interfere with magnesium absorption. That is more than three times the zinc upper limit. At ordinary doses the two are commonly taken together. We cover this in detail in Can you take zinc and magnesium together? Super Routine still keeps them apart, with zinc in the morning and magnesium glycinate at night, so the question never comes up.

5. Melatonin and other sleep products

Melatonin appears in many sleep gummies, drinks and "night" blends, so it is easy to take two products that both contain it. Label accuracy is a real issue: NCCIH reports that in a 2023 study of melatonin gummies, the actual amount ranged from 74% to 347% of the labelled quantity. Stacking products multiplies that uncertainty.

Use one melatonin product only. The Super Routine Night Pack contains no melatonin, but it does contain ashwagandha, which can cause drowsiness. NCCIH advises anyone taking medicine to speak to their health care provider before using melatonin, and says people with epilepsy and those on blood thinners need medical supervision. Ashwagandha might also interact with sedative medicines, so if you take a prescribed sleeping tablet or sedative, ask your doctor before adding either.

6. Omega-3 or vitamin K with blood thinners

This one is a supplement-and-medicine pairing, but it is the most important on the list.

  • Vitamin K and warfarin: people on warfarin need a consistent vitamin K intake from food and supplements, because sudden changes can increase or decrease the drug's effect. Do not start a product with vitamin K2, such as our vitamin D3 + K2, without your doctor's approval.
  • Omega-3 and anticoagulants: fish oil might prolong clotting time (raise INR). Most research found 3–6 g a day does not significantly affect anticoagulant status, but the NIH advises that people taking omega-3 with anticoagulants are monitored periodically. Tell your doctor before taking omega-3.

7. Two products that contain the same nutrient

The most common "combination" problem is not two different nutrients. It is the same nutrient from two products: a multivitamin, an immunity tablet and a separate zinc or vitamin D supplement. Vitamin D is the clearest example. The adult upper limit is 4,000 IU a day, and according to the NIH, vitamin D toxicity is almost always the result of excessive intake from supplements. If your doctor has prescribed high-dose vitamin D, follow that plan and tell them about any other vitamin D you take.

Minerals and common medicines

Minerals also bind to some medicines in the gut. These timings come from the NIH fact sheets:

  • Quinolone and tetracycline antibiotics (such as ciprofloxacin or doxycycline): take the antibiotic at least 2 hours before, or 4–6 hours after, zinc or magnesium. For calcium and quinolones, 2 hours before or after.
  • Levothyroxine (thyroid medicine): do not take it within 4 hours of calcium carbonate or iron supplements.
  • Bisphosphonates (such as alendronate): separate from magnesium by at least 2 hours.
  • Levodopa: iron supplements reduce its absorption.

We designed the two packs so the clashes above do not happen inside the routine. Zinc is in the Day Pack and magnesium in the Night Pack. Neither pack contains iron or calcium, so neither competes with a prescribed iron or calcium tablet if you space them. The Day Pack already contains 13 vitamins and 7 trace minerals at 100% RDA, so do not add another multivitamin, and copper is included to balance zinc. There is no melatonin in either pack, and every dose stays below its upper limit. See the full list on our ingredients page.

FAQ

What vitamins should not be taken together?

The main ones to separate are calcium and iron, iron (25 mg or more) and zinc, and high-dose zinc with copper or magnesium. Also avoid taking two products that both contain vitamin D, zinc or melatonin, because the doses add up.

Can you take iron and melatonin together?

Neither the NIH iron fact sheet nor NCCIH's melatonin guidance lists an interaction between iron and melatonin. Many people take iron in the morning, with vitamin C to help absorption, and melatonin at bedtime, which keeps them apart anyway. Do space iron from calcium, zinc, levothyroxine and levodopa, and ask your doctor if you take any medicine.

How far apart should I take iron and calcium?

Experts suggest taking them at different times of day, for example iron in the morning and calcium with dinner.

Can I take all my vitamins at once?

Many can be taken together, but minerals that compete, such as iron with calcium or zinc, are better spaced out. Fat-soluble vitamins such as D and K absorb best with a meal.

Which supplements interact with blood thinners?

Vitamin K can change the effect of warfarin, and fish oil can raise INR. Anyone on a blood thinner should ask their doctor before starting either.

/science/zinc-and-magnesium-together/.description: Yes, at normal doses. We explain the 142 mg zinc threshold, safe upper limits, the best time to take zinc and magnesium, and medicines to space.
/science/zinc-and-magnesium-together/.h1: Can you take zinc and magnesium together?
/science/zinc-and-magnesium-together/.inner:
Yes. For most healthy adults, zinc and magnesium can be taken together at normal doses. The interaction that has been measured involves very high zinc intakes of about 142 mg a day, more than three times the 40 mg upper limit. Keep zinc under 40 mg, supplemental magnesium under 350 mg, and space both from certain antibiotics.

Together?Yes, at normal doses
Problem doseZinc ~142 mg/day
Zinc upper limit40 mg/day
Mg upper limit350 mg/day (supplements)

Why people worry about zinc and magnesium together

Zinc and magnesium are both minerals absorbed in the small intestine, so it is reasonable to ask whether they compete. The NIH Office of Dietary Supplements gives a clear threshold: very high doses of zinc from supplements (142 mg a day) might interfere with magnesium absorption. Typical supplements contain 8–25 mg of zinc, nowhere near that level.

The two are also given together in research. In a 12-week randomised, placebo-controlled trial, 55 adults took 250 mg of magnesium and 30 mg of elemental zinc together every day, and the authors reported no adverse effects from the combination.

What zinc and magnesium each do

They are often sold together, but they do different jobs.

  • Zinc is a co-factor for hundreds of enzymes. It contributes to normal immune function, protein and DNA synthesis, wound healing and cell division. Whole grains, beans and nuts contain phytates, which bind zinc in the gut and reduce how much is absorbed, a point worth knowing for many Indian vegetarian diets.
  • Magnesium is involved in more than 300 enzyme systems. It contributes to normal muscle and nerve function, protein synthesis and energy production.

Because their roles do not overlap, there is no reason to choose one over the other. The question is only how much of each, and when.

How much zinc and magnesium is safe to take together?

Stay within the daily upper limits for both, counting every product you take.

ZincMagnesium
Adult RDA11 mg men, 8 mg women400–420 mg men, 310–320 mg women
Upper limit40 mg/day (all sources)350 mg/day from supplements and medicines only
Signs of too muchNausea, dizziness, headache, stomach upset, vomiting, loss of appetiteDiarrhoea, nausea, abdominal cramps
In Super Routine17 mg elemental, as picolinate (Day Pack)280 mg elemental, as glycinate (Night Pack)

Two details are easy to miss. The magnesium upper limit counts only supplements and medicines, not magnesium from food. And on a label, "1000 mg magnesium glycinate" is the whole compound: the elemental magnesium is about 140 mg. Always compare elemental amounts.

Watch for hidden zinc

Most people who exceed the zinc limit do it by stacking products: a multivitamin, an immunity tablet and a separate zinc supplement. Some nasal sprays, homeopathic products and denture creams also contain zinc. Long-term intakes of 50 mg of zinc a day or more can inhibit copper absorption, which is a separate reason to keep total zinc under 40 mg. Read more in 7 supplements you should not take together.

Best time to take zinc and magnesium

OptionHowSuits
TogetherBoth with a mealThe simplest routine. Fine at normal doses.
SplitZinc after breakfast, magnesium in the eveningAnyone who wants to avoid any competition, or finds zinc hard on the stomach
  • Zinc: can cause stomach upset and nausea, so many people take it after a meal. Keep it apart from iron supplements of 25 mg or more, which reduce zinc absorption.
  • Magnesium: absorption does not depend on time of day. Many people take it in the evening as part of a wind-down routine. Forms that dissolve well, such as citrate, chloride and lactate, tend to be absorbed better than oxide. Glycinate is gentle on the stomach.

Should you split them anyway?

You do not have to, but splitting has practical advantages. It removes any question of competition, it keeps a zinc-related upset stomach away from bedtime, and it fits how people already live: one routine in the morning and one in the evening. That is how Super Routine is built. The Day Pack holds zinc with the other trace minerals, 13 multivitamins and L-theanine with Panax ginseng after breakfast. The Night Pack holds magnesium glycinate with ashwagandha and omega-3 after dinner.

Who should be careful

  • Antibiotics (quinolones such as ciprofloxacin, tetracyclines such as doxycycline): take the antibiotic at least 2 hours before, or 4–6 hours after, zinc or magnesium.
  • Penicillamine: take zinc at least 1 hour apart from it.
  • Bisphosphonates (such as alendronate): separate from magnesium by at least 2 hours.
  • Diuretics: thiazide diuretics increase zinc loss in urine, and loop and thiazide diuretics increase magnesium loss. Potassium-sparing diuretics reduce magnesium excretion. Ask your doctor before adding either mineral.
  • Long-term proton pump inhibitors (usually more than a year) can lower magnesium levels.
  • If you are pregnant, breastfeeding, have a medical condition or take any regular medicine, check with your doctor or pharmacist first.

FAQ

Is it safe to take zinc and magnesium every day?

For most healthy adults, yes, if total zinc stays under 40 mg a day and magnesium from supplements stays under 350 mg a day. Check with your doctor if you have a medical condition or take regular medicines.

Can I take zinc and magnesium at night?

Yes. Magnesium is often taken in the evening. Some people find zinc unsettles the stomach, so if that happens, take zinc after breakfast instead.

What should you not take with zinc?

Iron supplements of 25 mg or more, quinolone and tetracycline antibiotics, and penicillamine all need spacing from zinc. Long-term doses of 50 mg or more can lower copper levels.

Does zinc block magnesium absorption?

Only at very high doses. The NIH notes that about 142 mg of zinc a day might interfere with magnesium absorption. Normal supplement doses have not been shown to do this.
